blocks.text: A pump manufacturer offers two 5.5 kW drive motors: one costs less and weighs less, the other uses more copper and steel but wastes less electricity. Which one is greener? The answer depends on how many years the motor runs before it is replaced, which is exactly the question carbon payback time answers.

blocks.markdown: A **linear** product ends in landfill after one life. A **circular** design keeps materials and components in use for as many cycles as possible. The strategies form a rough hierarchy: prevent the need for a new product first, then extend its life, then recover its parts, and recycle material last, because recycling destroys the shape and manufacturing effort that went into the part.

rows: Product passes to another user with little or no processing
Durable build, standard interfaces, easy cleaning
Faulty part is fixed or swapped in place
Accessible fasteners, modular parts, spares and manuals
Used product is dismantled, cleaned, worn parts replaced and tested to as-new standard
Design for disassembly, wear parts separable, core return scheme
Retains most of embodied energy of housings and shafts
Material is recovered and reprocessed into new feedstock
Few, compatible, marked materials; no permanent mixed joints
Saves primary extraction, loses shape and some quality
blocks.caption: Circular strategies, listed in typical order of preference (values are qualitative).

blocks.markdown: **Design for disassembly** underpins the middle two rows: snap fits or screws in place of permanent adhesive, standard fastener sizes, labelled materials, and a service life matched across components so that one failing part does not condemn the rest.

blocks.title: Carbon payback time
blocks.text: The time after which the extra embodied carbon of a more material-intensive design has been cancelled by its lower operating emissions. Before this time the efficient design has the larger total footprint; afterwards it is better.

blocks.latex: t_{\text{payback}} = \frac{\Delta E_{\text{emb}}}{\Delta E_{\text{op,yr}}}\qquad \Delta E_{\text{op,yr}} = \Delta W_{\text{yr}}\times f
blocks.caption: Carbon payback time. E_emb is extra embodied carbon (kgCO2e), W_yr is annual energy saved (kWh/yr) and f is the emission factor (kgCO2e/kWh).

blocks.title: Payback of a high-efficiency motor
blocks.prompt: A 5.5 kW shaft-load motor runs 4000 h per year. The standard motor is 90.0% efficient; the premium motor is 94.0% efficient and has 900 kg CO2e of extra embodied carbon. The grid factor is 0.40 kg CO2e per kWh. Find the carbon payback time and the net saving over a 12-year life.
blocks.answer: Payback is about 2.2 years; over a 12-year life the premium motor saves about 4.1 tonnes CO2e.

blocks.markdown: Payback time only decides the case when you compare it with the **service life**. If payback is longer than the product will run, the 'efficient' design has made things worse. It is also sensitive to the emission factor: as electricity grids decarbonise, the operating saving per kWh falls and the payback time gets longer.

blocks.title: Rebound and burden shifting
blocks.text: A design can look better on one metric while moving impact elsewhere: a lighter composite part saves fuel but may be impossible to recycle, and a more efficient product may be used more often. Always state which metric and which life stages you have compared.

blocks.title: Remanufacture versus new for a gearbox fleet
blocks.prompt: A fleet operator replaces 40 worn gearboxes. A new gearbox carries 310 kg CO2e embodied; a remanufactured one needs 95 kg CO2e (new bearings, seals and some gears, with housing and shafts reused). Find the carbon saved and the percentage reduction per unit.
blocks.answer: The fleet saves 8.6 tonnes CO2e, a 69% reduction per gearbox, but only if the housings are returned in good condition.

rows: Hard to recycle; higher embodied energy
Slightly heavier; more joints to leak
blocks.caption: Typical trade-offs when evaluating a design against sustainability principles.

blocks.title: Evaluate on life, not on a single number
blocks.text: A sound sustainability evaluation compares embodied and operating impact over a stated service life, states the emission factor used, and names the trade-offs, such as recyclability, repairability, cost and function.

points: Circular strategies in preference order are reuse, repair, remanufacture and recycle, enabled by design for disassembly, modularity and material compatibility.
Carbon payback time equals extra embodied carbon divided by annual operating carbon saved, and must be compared with service life.
Evaluating a design means weighing embodied against operating impact over a stated life and naming the trade-offs, such as lightweighting versus recyclability.

questions.stem: A pump manufacturer collects worn units, replaces the seals and bearings, re-machines the housings, tests each unit to the new-product specification and resells it with a full warranty. Which strategy is this?

distractorRationale.a: Reuse passes the product on with little or no processing.
distractorRationale.b: Repair fixes a fault in place for the same user, without a full return to as-new standard.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: dismantling, restoring and testing to an as-new standard is remanufacture.
distractorRationale.d: Recycling recovers material, not the formed housing.

questions.explanation: Remanufacture retains the shape and most of the embodied energy of the core parts and restores the product to an as-new specification. Repair and reuse involve far less processing, and recycling reduces the product to raw material.

questions.stem: Which design feature most directly supports repair and remanufacture of an industrial gearbox?

options.text: Standard fasteners and separable wear parts such as bearings and seals
A mixture of several unmarked polymers in the housing
Thin, lightweight housing walls to cut material

questions.correctOptionText: Standard fasteners and separable wear parts such as bearings and seals

distractorRationale.a: Bonding prevents disassembly and so blocks both strategies.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: access and separable wear parts allow worn components to be exchanged.
distractorRationale.c: Unmarked mixed polymers hinder recycling and offer nothing for repair.
distractorRationale.d: Lightweighting does not by itself enable repair.

questions.explanation: Repair and remanufacture require the product to be opened, the worn parts to be replaced and the rest to be reused. Standard fasteners and separable wear parts make this practical; permanent joints and mixed materials do the opposite.

questions.stem: An insulated storage tank with a thicker insulation layer carries 350 kg CO2e of extra embodied carbon compared with the standard tank. It saves 90 kWh of heat per year. The heat is supplied by a boiler with an emission factor of 0.20 kg CO2e per kWh. Calculate the carbon payback time in years.
questions.explanation: The annual operating saving is 90 x 0.20 = 18 kg CO2e per year. Payback is 350/18 = 19.4 years. This is the time after which the extra embodied carbon has been repaid.

questions.stem: A lighter redesigned conveyor roller carries 480 kg CO2e of extra embodied carbon and saves 60 kg CO2e per year in drive energy. The conveyor will be scrapped after 10 years. What is the net result over its life compared with the original roller?

options.text: A net saving of about 120 kg CO2e
A net saving of 600 kg CO2e
A net increase of 480 kg CO2e

questions.correctOptionText: A net saving of about 120 kg CO2e

distractorRationale.a: Correct: savings are 10 x 60 = 600 kg CO2e against 480 kg CO2e extra embodied, a net 120 kg CO2e saving (payback is 8 years).
distractorRationale.b: 600 kg is the gross operating saving; the extra embodied carbon must be subtracted.
distractorRationale.c: 480 kg is the extra embodied carbon only, ignoring the operating saving.
distractorRationale.d: Break-even would need a life equal to the payback time, 8 years, not 10.

questions.explanation: Compare payback time with service life. The payback is 480/60 = 8 years, shorter than the 10-year life, so the redesign gives a net saving of 600 - 480 = 120 kg CO2e.

questions.stem: A variable-speed drive adds 1200 kg CO2e of embodied carbon to a fan installation and saves 3000 kWh of electricity per year. The grid emission factor is 0.20 kg CO2e per kWh. What is the carbon payback time in years?
questions.explanation: The annual saving is 3000 x 0.20 = 600 kg CO2e per year. Payback is 1200/600 = 2.0 years. Because the payback time is short compared with typical fan lives, the drive is likely to be beneficial.

questions.stem: A designer replaces a steel bracket with a carbon-fibre composite bracket that saves fuel in an aircraft. Which trade-off should the sustainability evaluation record?

options.text: None; weight saving always improves sustainability
Higher embodied energy and difficulty of recycling the composite

questions.correctOptionText: Higher embodied energy and difficulty of recycling the composite

distractorRationale.a: Lightweighting can shift impact elsewhere, so this is not safe to assume.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: composites typically have high embodied energy and are difficult to recycle, offsetting operating benefits.
distractorRationale.c: Composites bonded to metal are usually harder, not easier, to separate.
distractorRationale.d: Cost is not a sustainability benefit, and composites are usually more expensive per kilogram.

questions.explanation: Evaluation against sustainability principles means identifying burden shifting. Operating fuel savings are weighed against the higher embodied energy and poor recyclability of the composite.

questions.stem: Using permanent adhesive to join dissimilar materials generally makes a product easier to recycle at end of life.
questions.explanation: Permanent adhesives make separation of materials difficult, contaminating recycled streams. Design for recycling favours few, compatible materials joined by reversible fasteners.

questions.stem: A manufacturer's grid emission factor falls by half over the next ten years as electricity decarbonises. Explain how this affects the carbon payback time of an energy-efficient machine and what it means for the design decision.
markingGuide: Payback time equals extra embodied carbon divided by annual operating saving in carbon
Operating saving is energy saved times emission factor, so halving the factor halves the annual saving
Payback time therefore roughly doubles if the embodied carbon is unchanged
Compare the lengthened payback with service life; a long-lived machine may still pay back
Efficient design remains valuable for cost and for locations with dirtier grids, but embodied carbon becomes more important, favouring lighter and longer-lived design
questions.explanation: The key is that payback is inversely proportional to the emission factor. A cleaner grid reduces the benefit of operating efficiency and raises the relative importance of embodied carbon.

questions.stem: A company designs an industrial air compressor intended for a 15-year service life. Describe design strategies that would support each of reuse, repair, remanufacture and recycling.
markingGuide: Reuse: durable build, standard mounting and interfaces, documentation so a second owner can use it
Repair: accessible fasteners, modular components such as filters and valves, spare-part availability and service manuals
Remanufacture: design for disassembly, replaceable wear parts (seals, bearings), core return scheme and test procedure to as-new standard
Recycle: material choice with few compatible alloys and polymers, material marking, avoiding permanent mixed joints and hazardous coatings
Notes the preference order, with recycling the last resort
questions.explanation: A full answer links each strategy to specific design features rather than listing the strategies alone. Credit is given for correct design enablers such as modularity, standard fasteners and material marking.

questions.stem: A designer proposes to replace a cast-iron pump housing with a die-cast magnesium housing that is 40% lighter and cuts operating energy of a portable pump. Evaluate this proposal against sustainability principles and identify at least three trade-offs.
markingGuide: States that the evaluation needs embodied and operating impact over a stated service life
Operating benefit: lower energy to carry or run the pump, which should be quantified using carbon payback
Embodied: magnesium has higher embodied energy per kilogram than cast iron, partly offset by the smaller mass
End of life: recycling route, scrap value and contamination of alloys
Durability and corrosion in service affect life and repairability
Conclusion supported by comparing payback time with expected life, noting the sensitivity to assumptions
questions.explanation: The marker looks for a balanced evaluation, not a verdict by assertion. Quantifying payback against life and naming trade-offs between weight, embodied energy, durability and recyclability earns the marks.
